newsitem.title: GERMANY: EMI takes stern line on lagging Euro preparations.
newsitem.headline: EMI takes stern line on lagging Euro preparations.

text.p: The European Monetary Institute on Wednesday said EU states were dragging their heels on getting their public finances in order for the planned 1999 launch of the Euro, and did not yet make the grade for monetary union.

In its first written report of 1996 on EU states' efforts to meet single currency criteria, the EMI said: "Progress in fiscal consolidation has generally been too slow. Most countries have not yet achieved a situation which, in a broader view, might be judged as sustainable in the medium term."
"Overall, the report concludes that at present a majority of member states do not fulfil the necessary conditions for the adoption of a single currency," the EMI said.

EU states have until the end of 1997 to reduce their public deficit and debt levels to three percent and sixty percent of GDP respectively, thus qualifying for the start of European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) on January 1 1999.

Many will struggle to do so, given high jobless rates and low public revenues in the region. Even the economic powerhouse of Germany is expected this year to exceed these reference levels, which are set in the Maastricht Treaty.

The EMI, the forerunner of the European Central Bank, said progress had been made toward fiscal consolidation in 1996 and developments on exchange rates and price stability were favourable. These are the other key criteria for the union.

The institute made no precise forecasts for the key year of 1997, although its report coincided with one issued by the EU Commission which predicted that 12 of the 15 EU states would make the Euro grade.
The EMI said many European nations -- including Germany, France and Italy -- must make strong efforts to meet criteria for the single currency.
Italian debt and deficit levels remained unacceptably high, the EMI said, so that "very strong and sustained action is required" to get finances into line.
Analysts said the EMI's strident words were more realistic than the positive tone in the EU Commission report.

"The Commission forecasts are based in many cases on a sharply sinking deficit ratio. The fall expected for the end of 1997 would be the biggest we have seen since second World War," said Elizabeth Legge of Bankgesellschaft Berlin in London.
"Italy is now the focus, but it is not the only one that will find it difficult to meet the criteria," she added.

DB Research's European integration analyst Ulrich Schroeder said it would be very difficult politically to convince Germans of the viability of a 12-nation Euro launch, especially given doubts over stability in southern European states.
Doubts on Italy may not be justified, "but that is the perception in Germany, and we have elections in October 1998," Schroeder said.

The EMI also said it welcomed efforts to establish a stability pact to ensure fiscal discipline after EMU but cautioned that the pact, which would sanction errant nations, was no substitute for convincing budgetary consolidation.

One-off efforts to trim deficits were also not enough to guarantee sustained fiscal discipline, the EMI warned. But the report did not refer to specific countries, including France's plan to use France Telecom funds to lower its deficit.
"It is emphasised that the improvement of the deficit by measures with a one-off effect does not ensure sustainable consolidation," the report said.

The EMI also spoke out in support of the Maastricht Treaty's requirement for membership of the European Rate Mechanism (ERM) as a prelude to EMU participation, noting that a majority of members of the EMI council supported this.
The ERM requirement has attracted consistent criticism from Britain, whose currency is not part of the system.
